summary:
Zabaykalsky Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed by President Putin; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets the baseline against which the krai is scored: same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and carry no specific legal protections.

Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and official Russian government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Penalties are severe on both tracks. The "gay propaganda" statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. Participation in the designated extremist movement carries 2 to 6 years and organising it 6 to 10 years; Human Rights Watch states that participants face up to 12 years in prison.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the 2023 Supreme Court designation as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges: one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison. A further 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols. The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

Enforcement has escalated in volume as well as severity. Cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling in January 2024, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and in December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. BBC Russian followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note contains no findings specific to the Far Eastern Federal District, so the national baseline is the only sourced starting point for scoring Zabaykalsky Krai. Nothing in the inventory establishes whether enforcement in the krai runs above, at, or below the national average.

Russia is treated by Human Rights Watch as a country from which protection should be offered: the organisation called on governments to provide safe haven to those fleeing the country after the extremist designation and the associated prosecutions.

Hostility is expressed through both criminal and administrative machinery at once. Charges are brought under the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying symbols and under the criminal code for participation in the designated movement, so exposure accumulates from ordinary public conduct rather than only from organised activity.
localsOnly:
Residents of Zabaykalsky Krai cannot obtain legal gender recognition. The 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, and gender-affirming care is banned outright, so the domestic pathway available in other countries does not exist for people living here.

Same-sex marriage is not available and no specific legal protections exist on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The propaganda statutes and the extremism designation apply to residents exactly as they do to visitors, with the same administrative liability under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols and the same criminal exposure for participation in or organisation of the designated movement.

Residents who leave the country face a distinct legal question abroad: the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement data, detentions, raids or prosecutions originating in Zabaykalsky Krai or elsewhere in the Far Eastern Federal District. Local conditions in the krai are unresolved rather than documented as either present or absent.

The penalty figures in the inventory do not reconcile on their face: one source gives 2 to 6 years for participating and 6 to 10 years for organising under the extremism designation, while another states that participants face up to 12 years in prison. Whether these describe different provisions or different offence categories is not sourced and remains unresolved.

No information is sourced on the availability of medical care, legal assistance or safe accommodation for transgender visitors within the krai, and none on how border or document screening is carried out at Zabaykalsky's points of entry.
